+Standalone evaluation (not part of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2)

+We report OpenAI's HealthBench and HealthBench Professional together. HealthBench has 5,000 health conversations, each with a rubric written by physicians. HealthBench Professional has 525 conversations with clinicians, split into consult, writing and research use cases.
+We use the HealthBench and HealthBench Professional datasets that OpenAI publishes with simple-evals (commit 652c89d), pinned by checksum: 5,000 and 525 conversations.
+Each model receives the conversation as user and assistant turns, with no system prompt and no tools, and writes the next assistant reply.

+A judge model checks the reply against each rubric item separately with simple-evals' grader prompt and returns whether the item is met. The judge is GPT-4.1 at temperature 0.5 for HealthBench and GPT-5.4 (low) for HealthBench Professional, matching the graders in OpenAI's original implementation.
+A task scores the points of the items it meets over the total positive points. Items with negative points subtract when met. We average over tasks and repeats and clip the mean to 0-100%.

+Our headline is the length-adjusted score that OpenAI reports. Before averaging, each task's score drops by a fixed amount for every 500 characters of reply above 2,000 and rises by the same amount below: 2.99 percentage points for HealthBench and 1.47 for HealthBench Professional. We also publish the raw score and the mean answer length.

+We report HealthBench by its seven themes and its five rubric axes, and HealthBench Professional by use case, by type (good faith or red teaming) and by difficulty. Breakdowns use the raw score, as in OpenAI's original implementation.
+We run 1 repeat per task for HealthBench and 4 for HealthBench Professional. Scores are the mean across all repeats.
+A task that still fails after retries scores 0 in every score and breakdown, and is left out of the mean answer length.

Evaluations we have retired or superseded. We keep their methodology here for reference and historical comparability; they are no longer part of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index or our active reporting.

personalityBench.fit: Firth-penalized Bradley-Terry; ties half win; 1000 bootstrap resamples for trait 95%CI
personalityBench.indexScale: mean of member trait Elo z scores, percentile1–100; Sycophantic inverted within Transparency
personalityBench.interpretation: Trait prominence/communication style, contextual preferences; not a uniform higher-is-better quality scale.

healthMethod.headline: length adjusted score; task negative rubric points subtract; overall clipped0–100%; slices raw
healthMethod.failure: task fails after retries scores0; excluded from average answer length

livebench.methodNotes: Single reported run per configuration cannot establish variance. Notes retain zero score when a task remains unmeasurable after one retry. Max effort is frontend metadata; complete prompt, temperature and token budget are not supplied in these exports.

removedRows.Name: Llama 4 Maverick
removedRows.Training compute notes:
22T training tokens per model card:

https://github.com/meta-llama/llama-models/blob/main/models/llama4/MODEL_CARD.md   

Maverick was trained using co-distillation from Llama 4 Behemoth. It isn't 100% clear that all 22T tokens used distillation, but we assume this for the time being.

Estimating training compute from parameters and tokens:
Compute = 6 FLOP per token per parameter * 17B active parameters * 22T tokens = 2.244e24 FLOP
(Implying mean throughput was 262 TFLOPS/GPU, or 13.2% MFU in FP8)


The model card also states that Llama 4 Maverick used 2.38M H100-hours.
The blog post gives a figure of 390 TFLOPS/GPU, but this may have been the utilization rate for Behemoth, or all of the models together. Using this utilization, we have:
Compute = 390 TFLOP/s * 2.38 million hours = 3.342e24 FLOP
(This value is higher than the compute implied by parameters and tokens, and suggests utilization may have been lower for Maverick than for Behemoth.)
